acts.title: What a biography has to do
text: A biography that works does four things, and listing dates is none of them.
It establishes the ___ : where the person came from and what that made possible.
It names the ___ only if they matter — and in some lives they matter enormously.
It identifies the ___ , the single moment after which the story could not have gone the other way.
It says what was left behind, which is the ___ , and what the person themselves would have called it.
And where the family continues — where the ___ are still in the same business — it says so, because that is what makes it a ___ rather than a life.

acts.title: Dynasty: the Churchills
tts: Winston Churchill is arguably the most famous man in recent British history. During a career spanning sixty-five years he became a national hero, and in 2002 a BBC poll voted him the greatest Briton of all time. But Churchill’s success did not come from nowhere. He was a member of one of the wealthiest and most powerful families in the country — the Spencer-Churchills — and he was born in Blenheim Palace.

In 1702 Winston’s ancestor John Churchill became the first Duke of Marlborough. He was a powerful man and an excellent soldier, and as a general in the English army he won several key battles across Europe, including the Battle of Blenheim in 1704. Queen Anne rewarded him with land in Oxfordshire and ordered that a magnificent house be built to honour his victory.

Winston’s father Randolph became one of the most prominent politicians of his time, serving as Chancellor of the Exchequer. He married the American-born Jennie Jerome, and the couple had two children — Winston and John.

Winston took after his father, who died in 1895 at the age of forty-five. He developed a love for politics and public speaking, and after working as both a soldier and a war correspondent he became a Member of Parliament in 1900.

However, the combative Churchill would probably never have become Prime Minister if it were not for the outbreak of the Second World War. Suddenly the country needed somebody who could stand up to the enemy.

items.q: What does the video say about the source of Churchill’s success?
o: It did not come from nowhere — he was born into a powerful family

items.q: Who was John Churchill?
o: Winston’s ancestor, the first Duke of Marlborough

items.q: What does the video say would probably not have happened without the war?
o: Churchill would probably never have become Prime Minister
He would not have been born

items.q: What did Winston do before entering Parliament?
o: He worked as a soldier and a war correspondent

acts.title: Dynasty: the Churchills
tts: In 1857 John Spencer-Churchill, Winston’s paternal grandfather, became the seventh Duke of Marlborough. Many thought he could have become Prime Minister if he had not died in 1883 at the age of sixty-one.
Winston Leonard Spencer-Churchill was born at Blenheim on the thirtieth of November 1874.

While he was never very close to his father, he looked up to him, and whenever Randolph had colleagues to visit, Winston would try to join their conversations. This enabled him to meet some of the greatest speakers of the time.
Churchill died on the twenty-fourth of January 1965. He is buried near his parents in St Martin’s Church in Bladon, two miles from Blenheim Palace.

He served for two terms as Prime Minister and won the Nobel Prize for Literature. His granddaughter Arabella Churchill helped start the Glastonbury Festival, and Princess Diana was a distant relative.

items.s: He served ___ terms as Prime Minister.
He won the Nobel Prize for ___.
His granddaughter helped start the ___ Festival.

tts: Today we want to hear about your regrets — the things you said or did that you really wish you hadn’t, or those missed opportunities that left you thinking, if only I could turn back time.

Greg from Glasgow: My biggest regret is ignoring my father’s advice to buy a flat while property was not too expensive. He even offered to give me some money for the deposit. This was about six years ago, when a small flat was just about affordable. But I didn’t, because I couldn’t be bothered to save up, and I didn’t think there was any hurry. Now even the tiniest flat costs a fortune. If only I had listened to my dad.

Jade from Bristol: A very good friend told me she was splitting up with her boyfriend. I had never really liked him, and I said, well, I think that’s a good decision, and to be honest I never understood what you saw in him. She was quite offended, and then the inevitable happened — they got back together. Now things are really awkward between us. If only I hadn’t opened my big mouth.

items.s: Greg regrets not buying a flat when property was cheaper.
His father offered to help with the deposit.
Greg says he could not afford it at the time.
Jade’s friend and her boyfriend separated permanently.
Jade regrets what she said about the boyfriend.

acts.title: What makes a life into a story
rule: A biography is not a list of dates in order. It is an argument about which of those dates mattered, and everything in the writing follows from that. The tenses do most of the work: the past simple carries the events, the past perfect reaches back to explain them, and the conditionals say what was at stake.
points: Open with the claim, not the birth
Say what the person is remembered for, then go back. “Churchill’s success did not come from nowhere” is the whole video in one line.
Past perfect for what made it possible
By the time he entered Parliament, he had already worked as a soldier and a war correspondent.
Name it, and use a conditional to show what hung on it: he would never have become Prime Minister if it had not been for the war.
Say what was left, and whether it lasted. A biography that stops at the death is unfinished.
Any sentence that could be replaced by a row in a table should be.
eg: He is remembered as one of history’s great leaders.
Open with the claim.
His success did not come from nowhere.
The argument of the whole piece.
By the time he was twenty-six, he had already been a soldier and a correspondent.
Past perfect, explaining.
He took after his father, who died at forty-five.
Relative clause carrying background.
If he had not been born into that family, his life could have been very different.
Third conditional, naming what was at stake.
He would probably never have become Prime Minister if it were not for the war.
The turning point.
What changed things was the outbreak of war.
A cleft sentence, useful for a turning point.
He served two terms and won the Nobel Prize for Literature.
Events, past simple.
After his death the family continued to play a part in British life.
The legacy.
If only he had written less and slept more.
wish / if only, for the reflective close.
acts.careful: A biography written entirely in the past simple reads as a list. The past perfect is what tells the reader which events explain which — use it deliberately, not decoratively.

acts.title: Emil Zátopek, 1922–2000
text: Emil Zátopek is remembered as the only person ever to win the 5,000 metres, the 10,000 metres and the marathon at a single Olympic Games. He is remembered almost as often for having run the marathon without ever having run one before.

He was born in 1922 in the north-east of what is now the Czech Republic, the sixth of seven children in a family with no interest in sport whatsoever. He was put to work in a shoe factory at sixteen, and by the time he first raced he had been made to enter by his employer, who had chosen four young men more or less at random.
What changed things was that he came second. Had he finished further down the field, he would almost certainly have gone back to the factory floor and stayed there.

By 1952 he had rebuilt distance running around a training method everybody thought was absurd, and in Helsinki that summer he won all three events in eight days. His wife Zana Ingrová won the javelin on the same afternoon as his 5,000 metres.

He was renowned for his generosity as much as his times: he gave one of his gold medals away to a rival he thought deserved it. After 1968 he was expelled from the army and spent six years working in a uranium mine. He is buried in Rossnov, and the training method is still taught.

items.r: opens with what he is remembered for, not with his birth
gives the background, and what it made unlikely
names the turning point and what hung on it
says what was left behind, including the cost

write.q: This is the last piece of writing of the level. Write a short biography of about 230 words of somebody real — a relative, a local figure, somebody you admire. Follow the model: the claim → the background → the turning point → what they did → the legacy. Use the past perfect at least three times, one third conditional, and one formal “Had he/she…” inversion. No sentence should be replaceable by a row in a table.
plan: the background, and what it made unlikely
write.model:
Rakhima Ospanova is remembered in one village north of Karaganda as the person who kept the school open, which is a smaller claim than it sounds and a harder one to earn.

She was born in 1931 in a family that had been moved there four years earlier and had not been consulted about it. By the time she finished the eighth class she had already lost both parents, and she was teaching the two classes below her because there was nobody else who could.

What changed things was a letter. In 1953 the district decided to close the school and move the eleven remaining children forty kilometres. She wrote to the oblast, in Russian, which she had taught herself, and somebody read it. Had that letter gone unopened, the village would have emptied within a decade, as three neighbouring ones did.

She taught there for forty-one years and was never promoted, having twice refused to move to the town. Two generations of that village learned to read from her, including my mother.

If she had been born anywhere else, none of this would have been remarkable — a competent teacher in a functioning system. She is remembered because the system was not functioning, and she was there anyway. The school is still open. There are now nine children in it.
